title: Artificial_intelligence_in_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election
summary:
Artificial intelligence has been developed rapidly in recent years and has been used by groups in the 2024 United States presidential election, as well as foreign groups such as China, Russia, and Iran. There have also been efforts to control the use of generative artificial intelligence. The 2024 United States election was the first to unfold amid wide public access to AI generators, which let people create images, audio, and video, some for nefarious purposes.

AI technologies were deployed across the election cycle, with applications in campaign outreach, opponent criticism, and heightened fears of misinformation via generative tools like deepfakes, though actual disruptions proved limited compared to traditional tactics. The anticipated avalanche of AI-driven misinformation never materialized. As Election Day came and went, viral misinformation leaned largely on old, familiar techniques, including text-based social media claims and out-of-context images. In a December 3 report about global elections in 2024, Meta's president for global affairs, Nick Clegg, said AI content related to elections represented less than 1 percent of all fact-checked misinformation.

Both Meta AI and OpenAI said their tools rejected hundreds of thousands of requests to generate AI images of Trump, Biden, Harris, Vance, and other candidates. The Election Assistance Commission published an AI toolkit with tips election officials could use to communicate about elections in an age of fabricated information. A 57% majority of U.S. adults said they were extremely or very concerned that people or organizations seeking to influence the election would use AI to create and distribute fake or misleading information.

When Vice President Kamala Harris brought up AI while debating Donald Trump on September 10, it was the first time a candidate had mentioned AI in a general election presidential debate. Carnegie Mellon University researchers designed nearly 600 questions about the presidential candidates and election process, posing over 12,000 question variations to a dozen models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Perplexity on a near-daily basis starting in late July 2024.
